title: Confessions of a Dangerous Mind
full_review:
Actor George Clooney shows talent as director of his first film, "Confessions of a Dangerous Mind" (Miramax). Too bad he's chosen a subject not worthy of such big-screen attention.

The stylishly shot movie is the story of crass TV producer Chuck Barris (Sam Rockwell), who lowered the bar for TV entertainment with "The Gong Show," "The Dating Game" and "The Newlywed Game." Charlie Kaufman's script is based on Barris' memoir in which he claims to have led a double life, killing 33 people for the CIA as he juggled the worlds of entertainment and espionage.
Since Barris is such a crude, sex-obsessed and self-centered character, his admissions of murder-for-hire are likely just a tall tale, but its casual depiction in the film is off-putting just the same.

However, Rockwell can't be faulted for his earthy portrayal of such an unappealing character whose career begins as an NBC page, then ABC employee before he gets the idea for "The Dating Game." When ABC rejects the original pilot, out of the blue -- or more accurately the black-- of night appears silky, smoky-voiced CIA operative Jim Byrd (Clooney), who offers to pay him for slaying enemies of the state. Tax-free cash more than patriotism motivates Barris, and soon he's left a few dead bodies in the Mexican desert, having no idea what they did to merit death at his hands. The stylized visuals and perky music track during his murderous jaunts inform us we are to appreciate this as black comedy.

Nor does Barris spare us accounts of his using and discarding women with no concept of respect, fidelity or any commitment. Drew Barrymore plays his main squeeze who for whatever reason puts up with his smug womanizing.
After ABC rejects the leeringly vulgar remarks made by contestants on the second "Dating Game" pilot, Barris cleans up his act and the show goes on to become a hit, followed by "The Newlywed Game" and, showing his utter contempt for his contestants, "The Gong Show."

Byrd meanwhile convinces Barris he needs to be an "assassination enthusiast" and has him use his chaperoning trips abroad with winning contestants as execution opportunities. His undercover contact in these situations is the mysterious, sexually available Patricia (Julia Roberts in an alluring come-hither mode).

But as his shows gradually tumble in the ratings and he develops a paranoid fear that a CIA mole will kill him, Barris almost self-destructs before taking matters into his own hands to eliminate the supposed mole in his midst.

The movie ends on a sour, nihilistic note with the actual white-haired Chuck Barris in 2002 New York City opining what kind of violent game show he would like to put on the air now.

The sleek visuals Clooney employs sometimes give the movie an intriguing film-noir look, but it's still hard to be compelled by the story of this coarse, self-aggrandizing celebrity. Since his superspy exploits seem thoroughly concocted, we are left with the chronicle of how he foisted his lowest-common-denominator programming on the American public. Frankly, it's not a pretty story that you would want to pay to see.
With its objectification of women, objectionable language -- including an entire scene based on screaming four-letter words -- and its nonchalant take on murder, viewers' time might be better spent in confession than seeing "Confessions."

Because of intermittent violence, promiscuous sexual encounters, crude sexual references, recurring rear nudity, some profanity and excessive rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
